title: Parity & Invariants
coreInsight: Instead of tracking every detail of a process, track a coarse property that remains fixed or changes predictably.
targetLearnerRealization: Instead of tracking every detail, track a coarse property such as parity that remains fixed or changes predictably under the allowed operations.
learningObjectives: Track odd/even state without computing every exact intermediate value.
Explain why an operation preserves or toggles parity for all allowed inputs.
Use an invariant to prove an end state possible or impossible.
Choose a property that is actually preserved or changes predictably.

continuity.openingCallback: Compress divisibility by 2 into two remainder states—odd and even—then track those states through a long process.
closingSeeds: Remainders other than parity can also remain fixed or cycle predictably.
A preserved total or coloring can expose impossibility without reconstructing a process.
An invariant needs a general reason, not just a collection of successful examples.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Matching parity means two numbers are equal.
Any simple quantity is useful to track even if it is not preserved.
Parity arguments require computing exact values first.

beats.purpose: Make an exact five-step search feel unnecessary once every move is seen to preserve evenness.
beats.expectedRealization: Starting even and adding or subtracting even amounts keeps every reachable display even.
beats.transitionIn: Divisibility by 2 gives every whole number one of two states. Track only that state while the display changes.
beats.transitionOut: We found a reachable answer without listing all 32 move sequences: the display never left the even state.
beats.whyNow: A move process distinguishes invariant reasoning from merely evaluating a parity expression.
beats.entryBridge: Ignore the exact path at first. Ask what +4 and −2 do to an even display.
beats.exitBridge: Every reachable result is even, and 22 is reached by +4, +4, −2, −2, −2.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A display carries an odd/even color while its exact number changes.
learnerPrompts: What parity does 20 have?
Does either allowed move change that parity?
Which offered display has the required parity and a valid path?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—22 stays compatible with evenness and is reached by a valid five-move sequence.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Both +4 and −2 preserve evenness. Eliminate every odd choice, then verify the remaining even choice with five moves.

visual.ariaLabel: A process whose display remains even after every add-four or subtract-two move

steps.title: Track the coarse state
steps.body: Adding 4 adds two pairs; subtracting 2 removes one pair. Neither move changes an even total into an odd total.

steps.title: Verify reachability
steps.body: Two +4 moves and three −2 moves total a change of +2.

resolution.takeaway: When every move preserves a property, the property can replace a large exact search.

beats.purpose: Show that a useful tracked property may toggle predictably rather than remain fixed.
beats.expectedRealization: Adding an odd number switches parity each time, so an odd number of moves flips the starting parity.
beats.transitionIn: A property need not stay frozen to be useful. It can follow a simple rhythm.
beats.prompt: A display starts even and adds 5 on each move. What parity must it have after 7 moves?

options.text: Odd, because parity switches seven times.
Cannot be known without the starting value.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—adding an odd number flips parity, and seven flips reverse the starting state.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Follow only the labels: even → odd → even → odd, one switch per move.

visual.ariaLabel: Parity alternates from even to odd across seven add-five moves

steps.body: Adding 5 adds an odd amount, so each move toggles parity. Seven toggles end odd.

resolution.takeaway: Predictable change can be tracked as efficiently as preservation.

beats.purpose: Replace example-based confidence with a general structural explanation.
beats.expectedRealization: Adding 4 preserves parity because four is two complete pairs for every whole-number input.
beats.transitionIn: Examples suggest the pattern. A proof must explain why no untested whole number can break it.
beats.prompt: Why does adding 4 preserve parity for every whole number?

options.text: Four is two complete pairs, so it changes the pair count but not the leftover-one status.
The last digit always stays the same.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—adding complete pairs cannot create or remove an unpaired one.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Choose the reason that applies to every whole number, including ones not tested.

steps.title: Even input
steps.body: An even number is all pairs. Adding two more pairs keeps it all pairs.

steps.title: Odd input
steps.body: An odd number is pairs plus one. Adding two pairs leaves the same single leftover.

resolution.takeaway: An invariant is established by the structure of every allowed move, not by a few examples.

beats.purpose: Name invariants after the learner has used preserved and toggling parity states.
beats.expectedRealization: An invariant is a property that stays fixed, while a predictable state rule can serve the same tracking purpose.
beats.transitionIn: The exact numbers wandered, but their two-color state either stayed put or followed a fixed switching rule.
beats.name: Invariant
beats.conciseDefinition: An invariant is a property that remains unchanged through every allowed move. A property that changes by a fixed rule can also compress the process.
beats.formalization: even ± even = even; odd ± even = odd; adding odd toggles parity
beats.memoryHook: Track what survives—or what changes on a schedule.

beats.purpose: Apply parity compression to five symbolic expressions and distinguish counterexample elimination from proof of the survivor.
beats.expectedRealization: A sample can eliminate options, but odd-times-odd structure proves 3mn must always be odd.
beats.transitionIn: Now the changing objects are expressions. Replace each positive odd integer by the state odd and propagate only that information.
beats.transitionOut: The sample pair removed four choices; the multiplication rule proved the survivor for every positive odd m and n.
beats.whyNow: The additional approved parity problem makes the difference between finding counterexamples and proving a universal parity claim explicit.
beats.entryBridge: Use m = n = 1 to eliminate expressions that can be even, then prove the remaining expression stays odd for arbitrary odd inputs.
beats.exitBridge: Since 3, m, and n are all odd, 3mn is a product of odd factors and must be odd.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Odd/even state colors replace exact variable values in an operation table.
learnerPrompts: What states do m and n begin in?
Which choices fail at m = n = 1?
What parity rule proves the survivor?
Why is one sample enough to eliminate but not enough to prove must?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—3mn is odd for every positive odd m and n.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use the sample to eliminate, then use odd × odd = odd to prove the surviving expression.

steps.title: Eliminate with a counterexample
steps.body: At m = n = 1, choices A-D are even, so none of them must always be odd.

steps.title: Prove the survivor
steps.body: The product mn is odd, and multiplying by odd 3 keeps it odd. This reasoning covers every allowed m and n.

resolution.takeaway: Examples can disprove a must-statement; a structural rule proves the survivor.

beats.purpose: Use a four-case parity table to infer an impossibility without knowing n or m.
beats.expectedRealization: Squares preserve parity, so an even square-sum requires matching input parity and therefore an even ordinary sum.
beats.transitionIn: Squaring changes magnitude dramatically. Ask whether it changes the two-color parity state.
beats.transitionOut: The even/even and odd/odd cases survive; both force n + m even, so an odd sum is impossible.
beats.whyNow: The approved square problem transfers parity tracking through a nonlinear operation and rewards case completeness.
beats.entryBridge: First prove a square has the same parity as its base, then test only the four parity pairs for n and m.
beats.exitBridge: The condition removes both mixed-parity pairs, leaving same parity without claiming n and m are equal.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The two-color operation table expands into a two-by-two parity-pair grid.
learnerPrompts: Does squaring preserve evenness and oddness?
Which of the four parity pairs make n² + m² even?
What parity does n + m have in both survivors?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Reduce n and m to even or odd, then test the four state pairs rather than exact values.

steps.title: Preserve square parity
steps.body: An even square is even and an odd square is odd.

steps.title: Keep the even square-sums
steps.body: Even + even and odd + odd are even; the mixed cases are odd.

steps.title: Read the survivors
steps.body: Both surviving cases give n + m even, so n + m odd cannot occur.

resolution.takeaway: Compressing infinitely many integer pairs into four parity cases can prove an impossibility.

beats.purpose: Repair the inference that matching parity forces equal values.
beats.expectedRealization: Parity retains only a remainder class and discards magnitude.
beats.transitionIn: The square condition forced n and m into the same color class. It did not recover their exact values.
beats.prompt: Which pair shows that two numbers can have the same parity without being equal?
beats.correctFeedback: Right—2 and 8 are different numbers but both even.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Look for two unequal numbers that are both even or both odd.

steps.body: Parity records only the remainder after division by 2. Many different integers share each remainder.

resolution.takeaway: An invariant deliberately keeps useful information and discards details such as exact size.

beats.purpose: Make property selection depend on the allowed moves rather than simplicity alone.
beats.expectedRealization: The sum is useful for a transfer-three move because it is provably preserved, while individual values are not.
beats.transitionIn: Parity is useful only when the operations control parity. A different process may preserve a different feature.
beats.prompt: A move adds 3 to one box count and subtracts 3 from the other. Which quantity is guaranteed to stay fixed?

options.text: The sum of the two counts

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—the +3 and −3 cancel in the total.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Write how each proposed quantity changes after one move.

steps.body: If the counts are a and b, one move gives a + 3 and b − 3. Their sum is still a + b.

resolution.takeaway: Choose a property by proving how every allowed move affects it.

beats.purpose: Assess direct parity composition without exact values.
beats.expectedRealization: Five odd addends have an odd sum because an odd count of odd states reduces to odd.
beats.transitionIn: Apply the two-state arithmetic to a sum whose exact terms are unknown.
beats.transitionOut: The number of odd addends, not their exact sizes, determined the sum's parity.
beats.whyNow: A near item checks parity compression in a familiar arithmetic setting.
beats.entryBridge: Pair four of the odd addends, then inspect the leftover one.
beats.exitBridge: Two odd pairs make even totals, and the fifth odd addend makes the full sum odd.
learnerPrompts: How can the odd addends be paired?
What parity remains after the pairs?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—the sum of five odd integers is odd.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Odd + odd is even; pair four terms and inspect the fifth.

steps.body: Two pairs of odd numbers each make even sums. Adding the remaining odd number makes the total odd.

resolution.takeaway: Parity can determine a sum without revealing any exact addend.

beats.purpose: Assess preservation plus reachability in a two-move process.
beats.expectedRealization: Only 20 is even and reachable from 18 after two allowed moves.
beats.transitionIn: Return to a moving display and use parity to eliminate before checking a short path.
beats.transitionOut: Parity removed four choices; one exact two-move check confirmed 20.
beats.whyNow: The item preserves the anchor method with new moves and a shorter independent search.
beats.entryBridge: Both +6 and −4 preserve evenness; then test the remaining even choice for two moves.
learnerPrompts: What parity is preserved?
Can the remaining choice be reached in exactly two moves?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—20 is reached by +6 and then −4.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Eliminate odd displays first, then construct a two-move route to the even choice.

steps.body: Starting even and adding or subtracting even numbers keeps the display even.
The exact route 18 → 24 → 20 uses two allowed moves.

resolution.takeaway: An invariant can narrow the search, while a final construction verifies possibility.

beats.purpose: Transfer predictable toggling from number parity to a two-color state.
beats.expectedRealization: Seventeen color switches carry black to white.
beats.transitionIn: Replace odd and even with black and white. The same two-state rhythm remains.
beats.transitionOut: An odd number of switches ends on the opposite color without tracing all seventeen positions.
beats.whyNow: A mixed representation tests the general state-tracking strategy rather than parity vocabulary.
beats.entryBridge: Pair sixteen switches into eight returns, then account for the last switch.
beats.exitBridge: Sixteen switches return to black; the seventeenth moves to white.
learnerPrompts: What do two switches do?
What remains after pairing sixteen switches?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—the token must be white after seventeen switches.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Every two switches return to the starting color; then handle the one unpaired switch.

steps.body: Eight pairs of switches return the token to black. One additional switch changes it to white.

resolution.takeaway: A predictable two-state cycle can replace a long step-by-step trace.

beats.purpose: Transfer invariant selection from parity to a preserved total.
beats.expectedRealization: The move preserves total 13, so a pair totaling 14 is impossible.
beats.transitionIn: Now the useful feature is not a color class. Track the total shared by two boxes.
beats.transitionOut: The individual counts wandered, but their sum stayed 13 and ruled out the offered total 14.
beats.whyNow: This mixed item broadens invariant reasoning beyond odd and even.
beats.entryBridge: Compute the starting total once, then prove one move leaves it unchanged.
learnerPrompts: What does +3 and −3 do to the sum?
Which option violates the preserved total?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—(8, 6) is impossible because its total is 14 instead of 13.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The starting sum is 13, and every move adds and subtracts the same amount.

steps.body: The initial sum is 4 + 9 = 13. Every move changes the sum by +3 − 3 = 0.
The first four choices total 13 and follow repeated transfers; (8, 6) totals 14, so it cannot occur.

resolution.takeaway: A conserved total can prove impossibility even when exact states change.

beats.purpose: Assess a nontrivial invariant where one move can change an exact count by −2, 0, or +2.
beats.expectedRealization: Flipping exactly two coins preserves the parity of the number of heads, so three heads is impossible from zero.
beats.transitionIn: For the final challenge, one move has three possible numerical effects. Ask what all three effects share.
beats.transitionOut: The head count may rise, fall, or stay fixed, but it always changes by an even amount.
beats.whyNow: The challenge requires deriving the invariant from cases rather than receiving it in the rule.
beats.entryBridge: Classify the two flipped coins as TT, HT, or HH and record the change in heads.
beats.exitBridge: The changes +2, 0, and −2 preserve even head-count parity, so 3 heads is unreachable.
learnerPrompts: How can the two chosen coins currently face?
What head-count change occurs in each case?
Which offered count has the wrong parity?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—three heads is impossible because every move preserves an even head count.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A two-coin flip changes the head count by +2, 0, or −2.

visual.ariaLabel: Three cases for flipping two coins, changing the number of heads by plus two, zero, or minus two

steps.body: All six coins begin tails, so the head count starts at 0, an even number. Every possible move changes it by an even amount.

resolution.takeaway: When every move preserves parity, an odd target is impossible no matter how the moves are chosen.

beats.purpose: Consolidate property choice, proof, compression, and conclusion.
beats.expectedRealization: A sound invariant argument chooses a move-controlled property, proves its behavior generally, and compares it with the target.
beats.transitionIn: Displays, expressions, squares, colors, box totals, and coins all became smaller state descriptions.
beats.prompt: Which checks belong in a reliable invariant argument? Select all four.

options.text: Choose a property connected to the allowed moves.
Explain its behavior for every allowed move.
Track the property instead of unnecessary exact details.
Compare the forced property with the proposed end state.
Treat several successful examples as a complete proof.

response.feedback: Keep selection, general proof, compressed tracking, and target comparison.

beats.incorrectFeedback: Examples can suggest an invariant, but every allowed move needs a general explanation.

resolution.takeaway: Track what survives—or what changes on a schedule—and prove why.

beats.purpose: Open the broader search for useful invariants without prescribing a successor lesson.
beats.expectedRealization: When parity is too coarse, other remainders, totals, or colorings may capture the move structure.
beats.transitionIn: Parity gave two states, but some processes treat all odd and even values alike while preserving something finer.
beats.prompt: If every move adds 3, parity keeps changing. What happens instead to the remainder after division by 3, and why might that be the better property to track?
beats.takeaway: The best invariant is the one whose behavior is controlled by the operations in front of you.

notes: Draft technique lesson authored from the approved S3 compact context packet.
The generated move puzzle establishes invariant reasoning before terminology; both approved AMC parity problems reuse the two-state representation.
Preservation, predictable toggling, general proof, property selection, and loss of exact magnitude are addressed explicitly.
All generated answers were independently verified by exact reachability enumeration or a second invariant argument.
No lesson-specific renderer infrastructure was added.
